utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to resume the examination-in-chief of Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Mandic and Mr. Tomic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic. Good morning, Mr. Tomic. Mr. Mandic, I'd like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Tieger, please continue

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic. Good morning, Mr. Tomic. Mr. Mandic, I'd like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. MR. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution's next in order is marked as ERN 0084-8625. It's an order of 13 June 1992 by General Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel Subotic at that time, the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number P ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd give you a quick moment for you to look at that document and then I'll direct your attention to item number 19 at the very end of the document, just above Colonel Subotic's name and signature. Paragraph 19 states that: "The commission for the exchange of prisoners operating under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall also function as an information bureau for providing information on captured persons." First of all, Mr. Mandic, does item 19 refer to the Commission for Exchange that we've been discussing during the course of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was envisioned by paragraph's 19 directive that the Commission for Exchange should function as an information bureau regarding captured persons? What kind of information was it supposed to provide and disseminate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this item of the defence minister's order, Bogdan Subotic, he informs that the Exchange Commission attached to the Ministry of Justice, but not part of the Ministry of Justice; it just relies on the Ministry of Justice. It probably refers to expert assistance or any other assistance to be rendered to the commission. And then the commission will act as an information pool or hub for details about the detained people to compile centralised lists and to inform the army or police structures when and how many people were in custody. As we said last time, a State Commission was established at the level of the government of Republika Srpska, and according to the opinion and the order of Bogdan Subotic, this commission was just attached to the Ministry of Justice. It was not part of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I ask you to turn to Prosecution's next in order, minutes from the 30th session of the government, held on 17 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as the minutes of the session indicate, the chairman of the session was Professor Djeric, the prime minister. The minutes also indicate those who were present, and as you may note, before the agenda items begin, the minutes note that among those absent with a reason was yourself.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn to the last page of the minutes, indeed the last paragraph. That paragraph states that: "The government has concluded that all measures be taken promptly for a more efficient work of the Republic Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners. With regard to this fact, it is necessary to secure the accommodation and other conditions according to a previous decision of the government, the Ministry of Justice is in charge." Mr. Mandic, do you recall the government's concern about the efficiency of the work of the Republic Commission for the exchange of prisoners in approximately the middle of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was that concern?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government wanted that the civilian authorities gradually take power in the territory of Republika Srpska, and this partially referred to prisons as well, or rather, the places where either POWs or other individuals were placed that had been relocated from places engulfed in war operations. Initially, there was some disagreement and some confusion about the responsibilities and competence of this State Commission for exchange of POWs, namely, if we think back that a few days ago we saw that at the first session of the government and the National Security Council, it was said that a commission would be established in the Ministry of Justice. However, after that, the government decided to establish a State Commission at the level of the government of Republika Srpska. After that, Rajko Colovic, who acted on behalf of Ministry of Justice, and he was an assistant in the pre-war government in charge of prisons, and penal and correctional facilities, issued an order on how the detained persons were to be treated, including the persons who were placed in isolation. After that, he unconditionally went to Vlasenica to take the position of the president of the municipal court, which is about 70 kilometres away from the government seat. In this interim period, until the appropriate chairman of the commission was found, my co-workers and I, during the preparation for establishing the Ministry of Justice, I did discharge some duties relating to the coordination of the work of the commission. The government concluded that it was not going well, and it seems to me that this decision refers to that particular issue. In other words, that the commission should have one seat, that it be granted conditions for unhindered work, which means proper accommodation and proper personnel. At the time, Vanovac was appointed chairman of the commission - I don't know what his first name was - from Ilidza, and he was, according to the hierarchy, a member of one of those lesser commissions for exchange and he was not even registered with the Ministry of Justice. Therefore, Minister Mandic and the minister of justice were in charge of reinforcing them in terms of personnel, to coordinate the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond work, and to allow this State Commission to start working later in this field. That is how I interpret these decisions and this conclusion of the government of the Republika Srpska, adopted at the session that I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I just ask the following. On page 5, line 18, the name does not appear, but my recollection is that it was translated to us as minister Mandic and the minister of justice. Could you please repeat what you said. Before you said that they were in charge of reinforcing them in terms of personnel to coordinate the work, which name did you mention? Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was a little bit confused. I mentioned my name, Momcilo Mandic, as the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Minister of justice. That clarifies the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you indicated that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now on the transcript -- perhaps I spoke too quickly. I said yes, as the minister of justice. And the word "as" is missing on the transcript. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you indicated that the government concluded that it was not going well. Did that conclusion that the work of the Exchange Commission was not going well include governments -- the government's concern about conditions in detention facilities and camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the situation in respect of conditions in detention facilities and camps that were safeguarded by the army and police? And if it's necessary to break that down into separate facilities, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can you -- can I please answer questions one by one, possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the situation in respect of conditions and accommodations detention in facilities and were guarded by or held by the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government, as an executive branch, was not capable to supervise directly the facilities that were safeguarded mainly by the army and to a lesser extent by the police. Various reports and information came from the ground about irregularities and inhuman treatment in these facilities in certain parts of the Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were at the time independent districts and the government tried to overcome this situation at the time when the roads were blocked and when it was impossible to provide free movement not only throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole but also Republika Srpska. So the whole territory was criss-crossed and it was very difficult to coordinate and to have direct insight into these camps. Therefore, the government tried in every possible way, and you can see here they even appointed the commissions and the people to act as envoy of the government to go on the ground, to review the situation, and to work in solving these problems. You can see here that it's mentioned independent district of Semberija, eastern Herzegovina, and others. Therefore, the problems were not only with detention facilities, but also with other aspects of everyday life in certain parts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall that the Assembly of the -- the Serbian Assembly, the Bosnian Serb Assembly, met at various points during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at those Assembly sessions, deputies or representatives from the various municipalities would gather at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that one place where there was an opportunity for communication about conditions in the field?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government on several occasions raised various issues that they were not able to resolve themselves. Since according to our constitution, it was entitled to propose to the president of the Assembly to convene the Assembly, to address specific issues, and that happened on several occasions. The point was to solve the vital problems of the functioning of the government, including, among other things, the detainees, the camps, and other issues, because they -- the government was attempting also through the Assembly to have the prisons and other facilities be transferred to the civilian authorities rather than the army and police authorities, which was eventually done in 1992, by the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what other ways did the government or representatives of the government attempt to address its concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commission was established in the government, tasked with visiting all places where POWs were detained in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think that one of the members, or even the chairman of the commission, was my assistant from the Ministry of Justice, Slobodan Avlijas, who was the assistant for prisons, and for this specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the government make known to the Presidency its concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, are you referring to the Presidency of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was communicated on a daily basis in order to overcome, as soon as possible, these problems that arose at the beginning of 1992, when the whole war chaos broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we were talking about government session in June 1992. In June 1992, through the beginning of December 1992, who were the members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska were Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president, and members were Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware, do you recall, Mr. Mandic, that -- of an Expanded Presidency that was formed during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were the members of that Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was published in the Official Gazette, and as a law, as far as I can recall, the members of the Expanded Presidency were the president of the Republic, members of the Presidency, the commander of the war staff, the commander of the army, the prime minister, the defence minister, the minister of the interior, and most probably the president of the Assembly, but I'm not sure about this last person. I cannot say exactly, but I think it was. There is an Official Gazette that it was published as a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall sending yourself a letter to the Presidency, or more than one letter to the Presidency, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dealing with what, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, a general question about whether you recall sending any communication, any letters to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was one of those letters a complaint about the failure of the Presidency to respond to a request by you to have the Ministry of Justice take over the competence of military courts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-1992, after consulting members of the government and members of the ministry, requested to have a centralised Ministry of Justice at the level of Republika Srpska. I asked the president of the Republic to review my request to merge, or rather, to have the military and civilian judiciary to become one, in order to become more efficient, and that would be beneficial to the legal security and to the rule of law in Republika Srpska. However, I requested that on two occasions, and I even wanted to have a meeting, and I also -- think I had a consultative meeting with the leaders of the military prosecutor's office and judiciary, but I had never received any response from the president of the state, either positive or negative, and that was one of the reasons why, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond towards the end of that year, I wanted to leave the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the second of those requests was in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that directed to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was addressed either to the Presidency or the president, but I definitely sent this letter for the second time, where I requested a unified or single judiciary to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness can be shown ET 0323-4335. Your Honour, in keeping with the Court's order, I note that that was a document that was disclosed on 15 November. It's a one-paragraph document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber wanted to be informed about any recently disclosed documents. Is there any observation in this respect you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The date is sufficient observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, is P445 a letter dated August 5th, 1992, directed to the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, underneath it says Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and signed by yourself, as minister of justice, the document to which you were referring a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you in one element, Mr. Prosecutor. It wasn't I who signed this letter. It does bear my name and surname, but it was signed on my behalf most probably by Slobodan Velasevic, assistant to the minister in charge of the judiciary. The rest is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Mandic. And who were the members of the presidency to whom you directed this communication when you sent it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, might it refresh your recollection about the membership of the Presidency at that time if I directed your attention to a portion of the interview between you and representatives of the OTP in March of this year? Specifically, if I could direct your attention to the page -- and Court's attention and counsel's attention to page 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, does the witness have the B/C/S translation of his interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When I say translation, Your Honour, we appreciate it's that rather mixed animal of B/C/S and English, depending on who was talking and who was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I said "version."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right to make that correction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the Defence have the B/C/S copy for the benefit of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Cmeric and Mr. Krajisnik have both got that, as far as I'm aware. We believe it's page 130 of the B/C/S, Ms. Cmeric tells me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, I want to direct your attention to what I understand is page 130 in the B/C/S version and page 116 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can see in the English translation, beginning at line 21, there is a discussion about the August 5th, 1992 letter to the Presidency. You state: "I have to explain that the resentment I had towards Karadzic and the leadership that ... because they refused that unified judiciary be formed. And I was of opinion [sic] that military judiciary was functioning quite poorly, if at all. Yes, they did reach some decisions and verdicts, but in my opinion, it did not work appropriately." And the question was: "When you say Karadzic and the leadership, who are you referring to?" Your answer was: "I think I sent it to the Presidency, Biljana, Nikola, Momo Krajisnik, and Karadzic." Mr. Mandic, does that refresh your recollection about the composition of the Presidency in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- I'm quite certain that Momcilo Krajisnik was not a member of the Presidency in this sense. When I was talking about the leadership, I did inform Mr. Krajisnik also about my opinion and request concerning the unification of the judiciary because it didn't function well. But not in these terms. The Presidency was composed of the president, Radovan Karadzic, and two members, that is, previously two presidents from the former Yugoslav system that were part of the earlier pre-war Presidency, that is, Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. Here, I either made a mistake because I thought of leaders in general, but Momcilo Krajisnik was certainly not a member of the Presidency in terms of this letter that I sent. It is true that I reported -- I informed the president of the Assembly on these matters even verbally, maybe I even sent him a letter, about this idea of mine that it would be good for the judiciary to be unified, and he supported my idea, because the courts functioned poorly, there was no harmonisation, many mistakes were made, and I, as a lawyer, a legalist, could not cope with that, and I thought that we needed to improve the judiciary in our state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the consequences or effects of the poorly functioning judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly consulted Mr. Krajisnik on this issue and he helped me greatly, because he was informed about the issue of the poor functioning of the judiciary, and it seemed to me that I had his support in this idea of mine to unify the judicial system at the level of Republika Srpska, because we lacked personnel, intercommunications, in order for the judiciary to function as it should. But I did most certainly inform him about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the poor functioning of the judiciary have an impact on the issue that was concerning the government, that is, the retention of people in detention facilities and camps and their ill-treatment in those facilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, and when I say "we," I mean the government, we received a lot of information from the ground, negative information, concerning camps, the emergence of camps, closing of camps, and the difficulty in the practices of the judiciary, and we made great efforts in order for the State Commission for Exchange to be equipped with cadre, to be based in one place in order for it to function well, in order to tour all the camps held mostly by the military, and some were held also by the police, in order for the State Commission to have an insight into the situation, to draw up a report, to submit it to the government, that would then address the Assembly of Republika Srpska on this issue, which in fact it did. The Assembly dealt with these issues on several occasions to solve the burning problems on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that the poor functioning of the judiciary exacerbated the problem of trying to improve the exchange of prisoners and other detained persons or their -- or the conditions that they faced in detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to make a -- well, it's an observation, objection. It will be both. But it's one that I should make in the light of Your Honour's observation the other day in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you have well thought it over whether it's needed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. I have to try and think quickly, but then that's the name of the game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the Defence would like to make an observation in your absence, so I have to invite you to follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I take it that the presence of Mr. Tomic in this open hearing is not a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on the clear footing that Mr. Tomic understands fully well and has throughout that he must have no communication with Mr. Mandic in relation to this matter. He's a professional and therefore I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this: That at -- and I'm speaking from memory, for the moment, but we can track back on the transcript if we need to. I'm trying to avoid that. But at page 14, line 16, Mr. Tieger asked: "Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the consequences or effects of the poorly functioning judiciary?" And then over a series of further questions, Mr. Tieger has been exploring what those consequences or effects have been, and he has done that most recently by way of fairly leading questions, which I haven't objected to as -- I haven't objected to the specific questions themselves as being leading. But my point is this, Your Honour, that clearly what Mr. Tieger wishes to do is establish that this witness informed Mr. Krajisnik of specific consequences or effects of the poorly functioning judiciary, and my observation is this, Your Honour: That it should not be must not, in fairness, be done in an oblique way. It should not be done by the foundation for an argument that there is a link then between a general question, "Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the consequences or effect of the poorly functioning judiciary?", coupled then with eliciting some of those allegedly -- those alleged consequences and effects by leading questions in that way. In other words, if Mr. Tieger and the Prosecution wish eventually in this case to argue that Mr. Krajisnik was specifically informed of consequences or effects, then the questions must be specifically directed towards that, and the witness should, because he's undergoing a species of cross-examination here, but that must be put fairly and squarely to the witness so he understands exactly what is being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is some kind of cultural clash of judicial systems. This is properly a matter reserved for cross-examination, number one, if there was an oblique reference or indirect reference left hanging, then counsel is fully capable of exploring it. Secondly, I have urged on repeated occasions to be permitted the opportunity, and indeed perhaps the courtesy, of completing my inquiry into a particular area. And I have not completed my questions of this witness concerning this area. I don't think it will be left oblique. I had no intention of leaving it oblique. This is really an unnecessary disruption. We would have gotten to that very issue in probably the very next question and now we've spent ten minutes talking about it. I'm going on for a little bit because I'd like to curtail this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not prepared simply to allow that. First of all, the cultural clashes between us are minor. All our judicial cultures have as a fundamental element the concept of fairness and fairness in examination of witnesses. There's no discourtesy intended and I do slightly, I must say, Your Honour, I slightly resent the fact that legitimate objections are characterised as discourtesy. We certainly do our very best to observe the utmost courtesy and apologise if we don't. But it is not reasonable to characterise legitimate objections by the Defence team as continually being discourtesy. The point is this: Mr. Tieger says that he is -- that if I hadn't interrupted, as he puts it, he says that he would have got to the point. If he would have got to the point then it's a little bit hard to see why he didn't get to the point more directly already. Because we have had four or five questions already. If he was going to put to this witness very specifically, as we continue to submit he should do, if it's his case that these consequences and effects were -- that Mr. Krajisnik was informed specifically and directly, then it's hard to see why that wasn't put several questions ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tomic. I think your main role here was to see whether answering questions would incriminate Mr. Mandic. This is a debate about the way of questioning the witness, and therefore, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and therefore, the Court -- and therefore, at this moment, the Court sees no reason to hear any observations from you. Mr. Stewart, the objection is denied. The way in which Mr. Tieger questions the witness is acceptable in the eyes of the Court. The witness may be brought into the Court again. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric says that Mr. Tomic had said that he used the phrase he "wanted to protect the witness." We only say that, Your Honour, for information. That's what we heard. And if that's -- well, then leave it in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it's a bit of a surprising moment, then, because no question was put to the witness at this moment which -- well, yes. If that last question would be the one, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not introducing a debate, Your Honour. I'm simply informing the Trial Chamber that that's what Ms. Cmeric heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, the question is whether the witness in answering this question would incriminate himself or would tend to incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say the following: My client has received a number of leading questions from the Prosecutor. I didn't want to intervene in the beginning, but I do see that now this is becoming quite serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, Mr. Tomic, the way of questioning the witness has got nothing to do with a possible incriminating effect. So would you please limit yourself to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. The leading questions put to my client elicit from him answers that could be fatal for him. I think that this constitutes abuse of the witness, and I would kindly ask the Honourable Trial Chamber to caution the Prosecutor Tieger about this. Because from time to time my client seems to be standing trial here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, if any of the questions would cause you to fear that by answering that question he would incriminate himself, you may draw our attention to that, but the way in which the question is put is not the relevant issue. And I'd like you to refrain from commenting on the, may I say, the trial techniques, as to how to examine the witness. You may be aware that the question of leading or non-leading examination-in-chief and cross-examination is mainly a specific technicality of the adversarial system, but as such is not something to comment upon. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger, after the witness has been brought into the courtroom again. Mr. Tomic, thank you for your observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I believe I had just asked whether the poor functioning of the judiciary exacerbated the problem of exchanges and of the government's attempt to deal with the problem of exchanges and conditions in camps. And you answered that question. Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik that the poor functioning of the judiciary was exacerbating the problem of attempting to address the exchange of prisoners and conditions in camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you tell him what you knew about conditions in camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often communicated with Mr. Krajisnik and informed him about different issues from the area of justice administration and different events taking place in Republika Srpska, and particularly in Sarajevo, where I had contacts. And often times I sought advice from Mr. Krajisnik and assistance in pushing for some of my ideas to be transformed into decisions and laws. Because the president of the Republic, under the constitution of Republika Srpska, under Article 83 of the constitution, at times of immediate war threat, could pass law decrees that would be later on verified by the Assembly, and it was with this procedure in mind that I asked from Mr. Karadzic and the Presidency to pass a law decree in order to unify the judicial system, in order for the personnel from the military and the civil branch to be unified, all of this with a view to neutralising the problems and the difficulties that the judiciary faced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Krajisnik what you had heard or were made aware of concerning irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, I mostly informed Mr. Krajisnik of all the issues that I was aware of, to consult with him on this particular branch of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution's next in order is an intercepted telephone conversation dated 1st of June, 1992, between Mr. Mandic and Colonel Vasinovic [phoen]. That is a document that was specifically disclosed, as I understand it, on the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P446. The audio will be P446 and the transcript, P446A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have this intercept among the intercepts given us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters inform us that they haven't got a copy of the -- this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's move on, in the interests of time. Can we turn next, then, to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next, then, and mark as the -- perhaps -- let me withdraw the previous exhibit. Mark this next exhibit as P446, Minutes of a session of the government held on 14 July 1992. And that's an ERN of ET 012454 -- I'm sorry. What looks like P446 is still going to wait because this was P64A, binder 13, tab 179. I actually have that listed, if it's helpful for the registry as P64A P65 binder 13, tab 179.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the document bearing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the document that bears that lengthy number that I, recited but that is the minutes of July 14th, 1992, the 39th session of the government. Again, that indicates that the session was chaired by Professor Djeric, the prime minister, and again, for the benefit of the Court, counsel, and yourself, I note that before the agenda begins, the minutes reflect the absence of three persons, including yourself. Mr. Mandic, can I direct your attention, then, to the last paragraph of the document, before the signatures of the government, secretary, and Professor Djeric. That last paragraph reads: "It was concluded that Ministry of Justice and administration at its first session is to inform the government on the work of the commission for the exchange of prisoners and to propose personnel solutions providing the normal working conditions of this commission."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether the Ministry of Justice and administration, whether your ministry did propose certain personnel solutions, and if so, what they were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, instead of Rajko Colovic, there was Rajkovac. I don't know his first name. I think he worked in the Ilidza municipality. He was to become chairman of the State Commission for the Exchange of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to refresh your memory, if it's my recollection is that we looked last week at a document of July 4th, I believe, some point early in July, reflecting the appointment of Mr. Vanovac as the president of the Exchange Commission.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would have preceded the meeting or the session of the government held on 14 July 1992, although it indicates that you were not present at that session. Do you know whether or not the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- last paragraph we looked at was a reflection that the government was -- had not yet been formally apprised of Mr. Vanovac's appointment or whether there were some other personnel issues of concern with respect to the functioning of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at that session; however, Nenad Radovic, my deputy, was there, and I think the government wanted to recruit responsible and professional people who would compile centralised lists at the level of regions, municipalities, and Republika Srpska, in order for it to function better in the future. I think that the point here was to reinforce this interim of personnel, and that is the State Commission of Republika Srpska. The appointment of Mr. Vanovac was not disputed, but the personnel reinforcement is emphasised here, as you can read from this condition. The government was not satisfied up to that time how the commission had been functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I then direct your attention to Prosecution's next in order. That's a document that bears the ERN 0190-4814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While this document is distributed, Mr. Tieger, I just draw your attention to the fact that at least in the translation, it's not Djeric, but Beric [phoen], who presided over the last meeting. But that might be a technical problem rather than anything else. I'm now looking at the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suspect we can agree at this moment that that's a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've made that correction. I don't believe there can be any issue about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be P446. The audio will be P446, and the transcript, P446A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm going to give you a moment to look that document over. It's a transcript of a television interview with Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a B/C/S version, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm advised there isn't. I think, then, we can proceed in one of two ways, and let me see which would be the most expedient. I think we should move on to play 446A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can play 446, but we can't play the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've got a backwards. Thank you, Your Honour. For the benefit of the booth, I think they need to specifically know that this is a Sanction document and they need to hear it verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then first listen to 446.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we know the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document which is contextually dated approximately the latter part of July, or the middle of July. That's about -- as I say, it's a document contextually dated, so it doesn't have a precise date in July. But I would say middle of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 1992, we assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters inquire: Do we have to read this document as it is played?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Every day, new camps are being opened for Serbs. At the same time, the Muslim side is attempting to accuse the Serbs of this. One of the greatest crimes against humanity. Recently a document was presented claiming that the Serbs have 57 camps for Muslims on their territory. Professor Plavsic was recently informed about these assertions at a recent meeting with top-ranking UNPROFOR representatives. Can you tell us how much of that is true. Plavsic: I heard about the 57 camps from -- I think I concluded that on the basis of a statement by Mr. Izetbegovic, which was frequently commented on in the mass media, and I really became interested in which camps they were. Naturally, since I cannot communicate with them, I requested UNPROFOR to convey us the names of the concentration camps from the Muslim authorities. Relying on the fact that there really are no concentration camps on our territory, when I made the request, I immediately said that if a single concentration camp exists in our territory, I'm prepared to go and visit those concentration camps at once with UNPROFOR representatives. They were really very quick in their activity and, after two days, I obtained a list of concentration -- alleged concentration camps in territory controlled by the Serbian authorities. This was done by Mr. Magnusson, who was in charge of civilian questions for UNPROFOR and we obtained a list not of 57 camps but of 42. Of these 42 alleged concentration camps, nine locations were cited which bear no relation to Serbian territory in BH, but are related to ... the nine sites are located in other states. When I say "other states," they cited places in Serbia and Montenegro. Of course, we did not take these sites into consideration at all and we very quickly asked the official organs of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to comment on the list. This is the information we got. On this list, which cites 42 alleged concentration camps, there should be a total of 58.810 detainees. After the list was analysed by MUP, it turned out that there were 8.251 persons in the said locations. Therefore, the difference is considerable, from 58.810, whereas there actually were 8.251 persons. Further analysis showed that these were not concentration camps at all, but regular prisons, and it is completely normal that prisons exist in peacetime, but especially in wartime. I could comment on each individually, because we have information for each individual prison. But I want to go back to these numbers. The great disparity between them, and just cite some examples. For example, the prison at Pale is mentioned with 2.500 inmates, whereas there are actually only 44. Or, for example, the Ilidza SUP, 150 inmates, whereas there are only 4. Or, for example, the sports hall in Hadzici, 2.500, whereas there are only nine prisons. Only one assertion related to the Prijedor sports centre approximates ... in their report, according to their analysis, there should be 2.600 prisoners. Here in Prijedor, there are actually 3.000 prisoners, and the location is Omarska. And those in detention are people who were sentenced by a judge, in accordance with the law and by regular procedure, to detention for a certain period of time. In this, in addition to this, it is precisely in this area, Prijedor and Banja Luka, that able-bodied men are located who are being divided into three categories. One category includes those who actively participated in rebellions. The second, those who assisted. And the third, those who financed the purchase of weapons. This is a more substantial number from this entire list. Otherwise, really there is no question of concentration camps. Naturally, I then informed Mr. Magnusson of the results of the research conducted by the MUP on the basis of the report we received from the Muslim and Croatian side, and I told him that whenever he wanted a commission, any commission, be it of the International Red Cross or the UNHCR, could visit those camps. I would be prepared to go and see whether they were concentration camps or prisons. MG: It's obvious that these allegations about the existence of 57 concentration camps for the Muslims on the Serbian side are merely an attempt at deception and to use untruths for propaganda purposes. On the other hand, Serbs are actually being imprisoned in concentration camps, which are predominantly run by the Muslims and about which numerous indications exist. Plavsic: As opposed to this rigged information, we have only partial information. But we do have the first and last names of the persons located in actual concentration camps. In this collection centres where they are in impossible conditions, there are able-bodied men, a large number of women, and in Bradina, for example, about 500 children. We have their first and last names. And you can see on the list here the names of the women are underlined and the years of birth, from 1977 and on, have been designated on the side. This is the period of childhood, and it can be seen that there are children in concentration camps. We have particularly had the opportunity to speak with some witnesses who have succeeded in fleeing these torture chambers. We have especially had the opportunity to familiarise ourselves thoroughly with the conditions prevailing in the Tarcin silo. We had - how shall I put it? - the good fortune in this tragedy to bring these witnesses to UNPROFOR members, and they testified orally there. MG: In addition, numerous concentration camps exist in Sarajevo. Plavsic: Yes, in Sarajevo itself. As regards Sarajevo, we have a list of prisons where the Serbian population is exposed to terrible abuse. People are taken away from their flats, and there is a method whereby they are returned to their flat, only to be taken away again after a certain time. Serbs in Sarajevo are hostages, both in their homes and in prisons. The prisons are the physical education centre in JNA Street number 3, the central prison, the Vladimir Nazor school for mentally handicapped children. That school, I'm told, is located in Hrasno, and they all refer to it as private prison of that soccer player, Edin Bahtic, where people are tortured in the most brutal way. They then throw them -- since the Miljacka river is nearby, they throw the dead bodies into the Miljacka. Then the basement vault of the Sarajevo commercial bank in Jovana Cvijica Street. They say that some man named Zlatko Lagumdzija is in charge of that prison. I want to say right away that this does not pertain to the politician, Zlatko Lagumdzija. Then the Viktor Bubanj barracks in Svrakino Selo and the Kosevo stadium linked to Zetra. They say that there are around 500 Serbs there. Of course the figure varies from day to day. Then the Velesic tunnel and brickyard. The Mladen Stojanovic student dormitories in Radiceva Street; Sipad, in Djemala Bijedica Street the garage by the Sarajevo commercial bank in Dobrinja, the nuclear shelter in Dobrinja 3; the prison at Stup, we do not know the facility, the tunnel of Kosevo hospital, the Stella cafe; the Alipasino Polje heating plan, the Aleksa Santic school; the Famos stadium in Hrasnica; the correctional institution in Pofalici by the tobacco factory; the Meteorological Institute on Bijelasnica, the police station at Bijelave, the Pavel Goranin elementary school. As we can see, 21 prisons have been cited here and that is all being checked in Sarajevo itself, which vastly outnumbers the number of prisons located on the entire territory controlled by the Serbian authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, does the Court wish me to proceed at this time or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how many questions you would have. If these were just a small number, then perhaps the witness has the video still clearly in his mind. If not, then we'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll exhaust the Court's patience as we go through this. I can begin and we can -- let me try to deal with one aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you can't -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in the latter portion of the video, Mrs. Plavsic addresses her attention to allegations of -- concerning Serbs held on the Muslim side. Were you aware of these allegations in the middle or latter part of July 1992; that is, that Serbs were being held by Muslims in Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that both pieces of information fall into the category of war propaganda. In my opinion, it is not true that the Muslims have as many camps and vice versa that Serbs had as many camps. I think it was just a propaganda war. There were rumours, which are only to be expected during the war, that somebody was holding a private prison, and that referred to the both sides. I'm quite sure that this camp in Tarcin, the so-called silo, did exist, and people were held there until the end of the war. I talked to some of these people. As for the remaining ones, I had no information about that. It was up to the MUP and the national security to investigate this matter, and Biljana Plavsic was charged on behalf of the Presidency to deal with this aspect of relationships between the warring parties. She had information. She communicated with international community, with UNPROFOR, and with the Muslim side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm satisfied that if we continue after the break, that I'll either be able to direct the witness's attention with a short interpretations or in any event we won't have any problem with recollection of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness and Mr. Tomic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mandic. The same for you, Mr. Tomic. You may continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can we turn our attention next to a document that came from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of the Interior, marked strictly confidential, a report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead, dated 17 July 1992 and bearing the ERN 0306-2180.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I note on the first page of the document there is a handwritten notation below the typed "strictly confidential, copy number 6," and 6 is handwritten, indicating to president of the Presidency and prime minister. Based on your experience, was a document such as this sent to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister as individuals or in their capacities as head of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the capacity of the president of the Presidency and in the capacity of the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the leaders of those particular bodies; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention, then, to page 3 of the B/C/S version and also the top of page 3 of the English version, which states as follows: "The army, crisis staffs, and war presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible. And they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." Mr. Mandic, you spoke earlier about irregularities and inhumane treatment in camps. Does this document sent by the Ministry of Interior to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister on July 17th reflect, generally, the kind of information available to the government to which you were referring earlier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Further down in the page, indeed toward the bottom of your page 3 and in the middle of the page 3 in the English, the document indicates: "It should also be noted that new territories are being liberated in combat activities and that even some Serbs are committing crimes, mainly all types of looting, in addition to the crimes committed by the enemy. Looting, as the most serious crime against property, mostly occurs during -" and the B/C/S word is "ciscenje", translated in the English as "mopping up," - "operations on which occasions paramilitary formations, military formations, and police engage in looting." Let me ask you this, then: What was the -- let me ask you: In what manner were new territories being liberated, if you know, at the time this document was prepared in the middle of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, these were combat operations carried on by the army, police, and these crisis staffs. I was not very much familiar with that. I suppose these were combat operations and ethnic cleansing of the non-Serb population in some areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to direct your attention next to page 6 of the English translation. And I'm afraid I'm not in a position to direct you specifically to the portion of the B/C/S where that is found, but let me begin by reading the first few words of that paragraph so that you can find it: "With a view to resolving existing problems and outstanding issues with the justice ministry." Can you find that paragraph, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The middle of page 10. It's the middle paragraph on page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That paragraph states: "With a view to resolving existing problems and outstanding issues with the justice ministry, it is also necessary to hold a joint meeting in order to address the problems of cooperation between the MUP and judicial organs in preventing crime and the shortage of judges for criminal cases, to reach an agreement on initiating proceedings for changing the duration of pre-trial detention (the Presidency should uphold the provision according to which detention can last up to 31 days) [as interpreted] and to resolve more quickly the issue of investigating judges, investigating centres, prisons, and especially round-up centres and the related issue of jurisdiction, so that the MUP in compliance with the ZKP, Law on Criminal Procedure, and the law on internal affairs can deal with individuals only until their trial or hand-over to judicial organs, which are products of the MUP's activity. Special emphasis should be placed on the issue of relocating certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because this does not fall within the competence of the MUP, although efforts are being made to link it to the MUP." Mr. Mandic, do you know the -- were you familiar with the problems to which this document refers in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does the document accurately state those problems or are there aspects that need clarification?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, especially in the war-struck areas, there were frequent incursions by paramilitary units or civilians who looted the property of persons affected by the war and took the stolen property back home. These were thefts and all the other aggravated crimes against property. The MUP were involved in combat operations was unable to prevent this and a way had to be found to prevent such practices that are contrary to the combat operations, be it the mopping up of the areas populated by the non-Serbian population or the areas where the non-Serb population was forced to leave their homes because of the war, and to protect the property left behind them. These were people who were basically criminals and committed criminal offences against property, looting and all the other criminal offences that accompany a war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document refers to possibility of reaching an agreement on initiating proceedings for changing the duration of pre-trial detention. Does that refer to the detention of looters or to the detention of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can glean from this, I think it refers to the looters of the property of non-Serbs. The people who came as members of the paramilitary units and committed looting in order to provide for a legal framework that would protect the property left behind in the areas and settlements where people, either during the war -- either because of the war operations or because of ethnic cleansing, abandoned their homes. I think that the minister here wanted this practice to be put in place in order to prevent the looting of the property belonging to the civilian population, that is, the population in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the figure in the translation which is 31 days, Ms. Cmeric assures me it's actually 21 in the original. There's just a -- some sort of typo or error there. It's right in the middle of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which ministry would have had jurisdiction, or which ministry or other body would have had jurisdiction over looters.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the criminal proceedings are instituted, the MUP is in charge of detaining people in custody up to 30 days. Later on, it is up to the civil justice administration. If these are criminal offences against property, if it has to do with all those criminal offences that have nothing to do with war crimes. So it's the MUP and the civil branch of -- the civilian branch of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know where in the law of Republika Srpska the 30-day period for detaining people by the MUP is embodied, or when it was enacted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is -- it was contained in the Law on Criminal Procedure, under the chapter of the responsibilities vested with the Ministry of the Interior. The MUP was the one that could order a 30-day period of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm a bit confused now. 31 days have been changed in 21 days and now we're back at 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Court is drawing our attention, Mr. Mandic, to the portion of the document which states that the Presidency should uphold the provision according to which detention can last up to what we are now advised is 21 days in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you have mentioned that the MUP had jurisdiction to hold people for 30 days if they so deemed. Can you reconcile that for us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking of the Law on Criminal Procedure from before the war. I am not familiar with this particular document where the War Presidency, that is, the Presidency of Republika Srpska, was able to pass decisions with the force of a law in order to set the period of detention, whether prolong it or shorten it. I'm not aware of the provision regulating the period of detention that was legally allowed at the time. There was a different criminal procedure in place for military personnel, and of course a different criminal procedure for civilians. I'm not familiar with the figures, and I might have made a mistake when I was mentioning the number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how would the Ministry of Justice be advised by the Ministry of the Interior that jurisdiction over detained persons had now fallen to the Ministry of Justice, in other words, that a particular period of time had elapsed and the jurisdiction now fell to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as is the case in all the countries where there is rule of law, you have basic courts and high courts. So this is within the jurisdiction of the courts, basic courts, and not within the jurisdiction of the ministry. If something takes place that falls under the jurisdiction of the civilian judiciary, of course, the pre-trial stage is within the competence of the MUP, that is the given public security station, they would inform the investigating judge, the investigative procedures would have their course, and if there is reason to believe that a serious crime was committed and if this perpetrator has a tendency to recurring criminal offences, then this will be given to the jurisdiction of the investigating judge of a competent court in that period. I know that for those crimes where sentences exceeding ten years would be provided for, the jurisdiction would lie with the basic courts, whereas for the sentences exceeding ten years of prison, district courts would have the jurisdiction. So these are -- what we are talking about here are crimes within the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you referred to the reference to the investigating judge. Before the case was referred to an investigating judge, how long could someone be held in detention by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether it was up to 30 days or up to 21 days, as it says here in the document. But the MUP had the obligation to inform the investigating judge of an on-site investigation that was being carried out or of a crime. And the MUP had the obligation to inform the duty investigating judge the moment they learnt of the crime having been committed, and the investigating judge would immediately carry out an on-site investigation himself or would actually task the MUP employees to do that in his stead. Once the file is complete, it is forwarded to the investigating judge for some further administrative actions to be taken, and then it's forwarded to the prosecutor's office for an indictment to be issued. This was a procedure that was valid both before the war and during the war, that is, after the war, the one that we took over in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Stanisic or any other representative of the Ministry of the Interior in an effort to resolve the existing problems and outstanding issues referred to in the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would meet quite often, both the two of us, both at the meetings of the government, where we discussed all these issues, including the criminality, the crimes that were on the increase in the war-struck areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we be clear, there, whether -- I'm not sure, but I believe that a little while ago the witness indicated he hadn't had an opportunity or perhaps not a recent opportunity to read this whole document. If Mr. Tieger's question there about meeting to resolve the existing problems and outstanding issues referred to in the document relate to the passages which have been put to the witness then there's no problem. If it's intended to extend more widely, then the witness should have an opportunity, if he needs it, of considering the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's fair, and my question was only directed to those issues and problems that were contained in the portion of the document we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear, then, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long had you known Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had known him for a long time. We studied together at the police academy and graduated at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you -- did you engage in sports? I know you were a well-known sportsman. Did you -- were you and Mr. Stanisic involved in sporting activities together?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were engaged in judo, and I don't want to sound immodest, but I was among the top sportsmen, whereas he was among the best at the republic level. So I won the European medals, the Balkan championships medals, and other regional medals, whereas he reached only the level of being the champion in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you and Mr. Stanisic friends from before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first began exchanging information with Mr. Stanisic about the problems that are reflected in the portions of the document we looked at?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But if I may try and clarify something, Mr. Prosecutor. These problems were constant and permanently present and we constantly discussed them at the government sessions and in our one-on-one meetings, and we tried to solve this problem of lawlessness that accompanied the beginning of the war. Since the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina was criss-crossed and engulfed by the war operations, it was very difficult for the civilian judiciary and the civilian authorities in the government to exercise their powers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've referred to the problem of looting in connection with that portion of the document which we've looked at on English page 6 and B/C/S page 10, and we've previously looked at that portion of the document on page 3 which discusses the round-up or capture of as many Muslim civilians as possible. In the course of your discussions with Mr. Stanisic, did the two of you focus on one of those problems more than the other? Did you consider one of those problems more significant than the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, we had tremendous problems with these war presidencies. Those were civilians who organised the authority, the army, the paramilitary, and the reserve forces in individual municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if you look at page 3 of the B/C/S version, it says that the army and Crisis Staff, or rather, war presidencies request that as many Muslims should be captured as possible, which is totally inappropriate and contrary to all international conventions. That was one of the most serious problems for the civilian authorities to function properly in Republika Srpska. And the consequence of all that was looting of property and everything else that those people left behind without any protection. The paramilitary forces, civilians, and everyone else who -- criminals who were involved in all this, the old and the new criminals, took the advantage of this war and this misfortune to loot other people's property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for one clarification of this last answer. You've drawn our attention to that specific portion of this document which reads: "The army, crisis staffs, and war presidencies..." Do you agree that reading this document would say that it was not just the locals, to say it that way, crisis staffs, War Presidency, but the army as well, which had requested that the army, that is, themselves, round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible? Your answer in the totality of your last answer suggests that it was only the local -- these were only the local people who were asked this, but I clearly see the army mentioned as well, which is not a local organisation, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Crisis Staff, or rather, the war presidencies that were composed of civilians in authority requests the military and the armed forces to have as many Muslims as possible ethnically cleansed. It was not the army that requested that but the army was requested to do that. I don't think that this is a properly composed sentence on page 3 of the translation. Sorry, of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in the original, I see the first word beings "vojska," isn't it? That's the usual reference to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two things excluded each other. It cannot be that the army asked the army to round up as many people. So this is a poorly phrased sentence. You either ask the army to do it or vice versa. You cannot have it both ways. Because the hierarchy and the place of the army in the hierarchy is well-known. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Theoretically that may be right, but is it unimaginable that the army, crisis staffs, and war presidencies take the same view and request that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible? A shared opinion on what the army should do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what should be understood by reading this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On page 10 of your version and page 6 of the English, Ministry of Interior also expresses concern about the issue of relocating certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because although that does not fall within the competence of the MUP, efforts were being made to link it to the MUP. Did you and Mr. Stanisic talk about this concern?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. I think that was the conflict of jurisdictions between the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in what way did the concern over the relocation of citizens and villages relate to the detention of persons, either -- well, non-Serbs, referred to in the other portions of the document we reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army set up collection centres, as did the police, and the people from war-torn areas were brought there, and they were either exchanged or ethnic cleansing was conducted where there were no war operations, whereas from other locations, in my view, the population was removed from the war operation zones. In all war operations, the police was subordinated to the army, and the army was superior to the police. That is what is known as the state of immediate peril of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to the second paragraph of page 4 in the English version, and I believe the second paragraph of page 5 of the B/C/S, the last sentence of both paragraphs. That states, after describing some of the activities of the MUP forces, including organisation into wartime units, states: "In other words, cooperation was immediately achieved with other parts of the Serb defence forces, that is, with the army." Was the MUP cooperating with the army in combat operations and other activities related to events in the field?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next to a document dated July 20th, 1992, from the security service centre of Banja Luka, and directed to the MUP of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the minister, the ERN is ET 0324-6719.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, that document is signed by the head of the security services centre in Banja Luka, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, and it begins by indicating that during the months of April, May, June, and July of 1992, in the autonomous region of Krajina, there were armed conflicts, and stating that: "We have informed you about the progress and the results of those conflicts on a regular basis." And then in the second paragraph of the document it goes on to note: "However, during these conflicts, representatives of army of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and police arrested a great number of citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality who were, depending on the number and the circumstances in the field, sent to various buildings, like schools, centres, factory facilities, open-area (playgrounds) and so on. According to our information, this situation involves several thousands of mostly military age men. They were subject to operational procedure by military service, service for national and public security, which then carried out selection of the person detained. After the operational procedure, three categories were determined. First and second category of are security interest to us, and their activity can be classified as legal responsibility (active participants in enemy formations during the armed conflicts, illegal suppliers and financiers of arming of Muslim and Croatian people, secret and organised preparation of armed rebellion and elimination of Serbian individuals and so on. While the third category is made of adult men on which, so far, the service doesn't have any information of security interest for us so they can be treated as hostages." And then on the next page, the second page of the English translation and the third page of the B/C/S document that you have before you, Mr. Zupljanin goes on to describe the positions that he believes should be adopted, including the exchange of military-aged men of no security interest who can be treated only as hostages. That's contained in item number 3. "Try to exchange military age men of no security interest to us, who can be treat only as hostages, for citizens of Serbian nationality who have been detained in camps held by Muslim-Croatian forces, according to the same criteria." Now, in a document we previously looked at, that is, the video of Mrs. Plavsic, she refers to the categorisation of men. Here we see the categorisation of non-Serbs of no security -- who have been detained and who are of no security interest. Was that a problem that you and Mr. Stanisic discussed during the course of your discussions about issues that needed to be addressed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic and I discussed the problems of crime, theft of property and destruction of property that had been abandoned either forcibly or voluntarily. As for these matters concerning the relationship between the army and the police, I don't remember that we ever discussed this topic. These are, after all, the things that were under the jurisdiction of the army and the police respectively. You can probably ask me, as an experienced policeman, what my opinion was or is, but it is obvious that this pertains to the relationship between the military and the police or the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But does the categorisation of persons taken into custody and held in detention refer to the investigative processes that were conducted by the MUP before an investigative judge referral to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the Law on Criminal Procedure, there is no age category of people. It just speaks about the category of crime and the seriousness of crime committed.
