Here we have captured persons who were kept in isolation in school buildings and other buildings where they were kept by the police, and this is where the conflict occurred between the military and the police, and apparently our centre was requested to determine whether the police or the military were to safeguard these camps, and they even activated the reserve and retired policemen for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, on the 25th of November, on page 42, you told us that the entire government, led by Mr. Djeric, requested that people not be detained, that civilians not be detained or deprived of liberty who had been incorporated into the war.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was he referring to the civilians who are - non-Serb civilians - who are indicated in Mr. Zupljanin's letter of July 20th and in the previous report we saw from the Ministry of the Interior on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we turn next to the minutes of the 36th session of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government held on 4 July 1992. That bears an ERN of ET 0124-5416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you proceed, this last document you gave to us even has page 3 out of 2, which is, I do know that the Prosecution now and then does the -- or tries to do what's very difficult. I just wanted to draw your attention that these can create at other moments more confusion, as it does now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in this session conducted on the 4th of July, 1992, again the chairman was Professor Djeric, the prime minister, the document begins by noting who was present and who was absent, and I note that it indicates that absent from the session with a reason were a number of persons, including yourself.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn, Mr. Mandic, who agenda item number 8. That is the last agenda item of the session. And it states as follows: "The question has been raised whether there are agreed criteria regarding the moving out of the Muslims' population from the territory of the Serb Republic of BH. It has been concluded that the government has not until now had a point of view on this matter. The Ministry of the Interior is entrusted with preparing information on this issue that the government would consider and take the appropriate standpoint." First of all, Mr. Mandic, was this one of the responses by the government, or reactions by the government, to information of the type we've just been looking at reflected in the July 20th, 1992 document, or July 17th, 1992 document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution's next in order is a document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you. My apologies. Prosecution's next in order is a document dated 8 August 1992, bearing the heading "Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo." And bearing the ERN ET 0124-5167.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, P450, dated August 8th, 1992, is signed by the deputy minister for police affairs and tasks, Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the date, August 8th, 1992, do you recall that on August 5th, 1992, reporters gained access to the Omarska camp in Prijedor and publicised details of their visit in the international press?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall generally an international outcry about non-Serb civilians -- about allegations that non-Serb civilians were being held in Serb detention facilities around that time, that is, early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention to the first paragraph of Mr. Kovac's document. That states: "With the aim to resolve problems arising from the detention of other peoples -- nations in certain facilities and collection centres in the zones of war activities, apart from the measures already taken by the government and its authorised ministries, I propose the following: That the status of these people be legally changed in compliance with international conventions on refugees, prisoners of war, et cetera." And then if you'll look at the following paragraphs of the document, Mr. Kovac discusses the involvement of members of the MUP in capturing or arranging for the accommodation of captured persons, and he also discusses problems, as he sees it, in categorisation. Does the concern expressed by Mr. Kovac reflect a more general intensified concern about the detention of non-Serbs and their treatment after the international outcry following the disclosures about the camps in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that was really the case. Let me tell you,

utterances.speaker: MR. PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: It is not usual for an assistant to the minister to address directly the president of the Serbian Republic and the prime minister of the Serbian Republic. It seems to me that this was a responsibility that was to be assumed in relation to the previous period. Under the law governing the MUP, Tomo Kovac was not allowed to address a letter either to the president of the Republic or the prime minister. He could have contacted only his minister, who would then be the most appropriate person to submit such a material expressing his grave concern to other competent institutions. So it seems to me that there are other matters at work here. This is not a legal way of communicating by an assistant to the minister who is maybe the fourth or fifth person down the hierarchy in the MUP, and with the president and the prime minister being the end receivers of the communication. That's why I think that there are other things at work here. Under the law on internal affairs, no one can address without the approval of the minister the higher-level institutions in government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask for a clarification of this answer, unless you'd further ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say this is not what was proper in the structure. Nevertheless, we see a document which does so. Then you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're suggesting that there must be something else. First of all, do you consider what's written in this letter to be not correct? I'm not talking about the formal procedure, but I'm talking just about the content of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not suspect that what has been mentioned here is not true, that there were practices contrary to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and other human rights instruments. What seems to me here is that this concern expressed by Tomo Kovac is quite a hypocritical one, because he was an assistant minister at the time, and we are at a moment when the international community had already established the situation as it was, that he is now putting himself into the capacity of interpreting international human rights instruments. And we've seen dozens of documents already asking for the categorisation -- for a proper categorisation of people. So I do have my doubts concerning this being a true and sincere expression of remorse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was just as well aware before the facts were established of the situation as he describes in that letter and that you say it's hypocritical to draw the attention to this as something improper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he knew, as deputy minister for police affairs and tasks, was this general knowledge on the government level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We used to receive such information on a daily basis and launch initiatives for such practices to be prevented or reduced, as far as possible. And I mean the expulsion of civilians. Tomo Kovac was an assistant to the ministry, Your Honour, not a deputy minister. He was directly in charge of the armed forces of MUP, and as such, he had direct information, knowledge, and authority to engage the armed forces of MUP on the ground and to coordinate this activity with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe. Ms. Cmeric tells me that there is a translation issue in relation to the very last words that appear on this document. Perhaps I simply make that comment and reserve that point and we'll take it up rather than discuss it in any more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if it is a translation issue, is there any problem? We have to listen to the tape if we do not resolve it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'm just nervous. It's simply this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could have the witness to repeat that part of his question, see whether it's -- could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, that's not entirely the point. Fact is if there's a translation error, there is a translation error and the witness is not the person to resolve this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if we ask him to repeat his answer, we'll see whether we get a different translation from we got before. I take it, translation into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. We will then -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rather than drawing the attention of the witness to the point you have problems with. Could you indicate in English from what part -- non-contentious part you'd like him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It really starts well it's the answer that begins, "We used to receive such information on a daily basis." It's that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you, Mr. Mandic, repeat your answer. I asked whether it was general knowledge on the government level at that time. And then you started saying: "We used to receive such information." Could you please repeat that answer, because there seems to be some problem. You said: "We used to receive such information on a daily basis and launch ..." Could you repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I -- there may be some ambiguity, and before we begin, I want to be make sure we resolve that. I understood Ms. Cmeric through Mr. Stewart to be referring to a document and not the response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then, yes, now I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought I had made that clear, but my apologies. Your Honour, I -- it's just this, perhaps I'm being overly nervous. It's a distinction between deputy and assistant. It's just that. What I'm about to say about the translation is in fact consistent with what the witness has said in -- or the way the translation -- interpretation came across this morning. But Ms. Cmeric tells me that whereas it says "deputy minister" at the end of this document in the English translation that she suggests that "assistant minister" is the appropriate translation. That is It's just that that is actually consistent with the answer that the witness gave in that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course in my question I refer to the translation of this document when I said "deputy minister" which was corrected by the witness. It's now been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now been clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could turn next to the minutes of the 46th session of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government held on 9 August 1992, bearing the ERN ET 0124-5481.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as you can see, Prosecution's 451 reflects the minutes of a session of the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on 9 August 1992. And as we see in the notations following the minutes, that is a session at which you were president -- you were present, excuse me, as is indicated in addition to the prime minister, the following ministers were present, Ljubomir Zukovic, Petra Markovic, Momcilo Mandic, and then it goes on to indicate others who were present. And I should indicate that, although the English translation says in addition to the prime minister, the following ministers were present, it also indicates in the last paragraph before the agenda items that in fact Mr. Djeric was absent and the session was chaired by the deputy prime minister. In any event, Mr. Mandic, if I could ask you to turn to agenda item number 12. That items states: "The government formed two commissions consisting of representatives from the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Judiciary and Administration. The commission's task is to gain knowledge through responsible state organs about the status of people in concentration centres and other sheltering facilities. To speed up the procedure of categorising these people, establishing responsibility and sanctions." And does the witness still have P450 in front of him? If not, could that be placed in front of him. First of all, Mr. Mandic, what was the mandate or the responsibility of the two commissions reflected in agenda item number 12?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of the commission was to gain knowledge through responsible state organs about the status of people in concentration centres and other sheltering facilities, to speed up the procedure of categorising these people to establish their responsibility and sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I note that handwritten in the upper right-hand corner of P450, Mr. Kovac's letter of August 8th, 1992, is a notation that says: "Combine team of the police and judiciary or judicature are to inspect 1, categorisation; 2, jurisdiction of organs; and 3, something illegible, and sanctions." First of all, you may be able to decipher the ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To speed up the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those are the words that immediately precede sanctions in number three of the handwritten notation on Mr. Kovac's letter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, is there a difference --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, we still think that's incomplete. It's -- it might be best, Mr. Tieger said those are the words immediately precede sanction in the handwritten notation. It might be best simply to allow the witness to tell us what the whole of that handwritten entry says so we've got it a hundred per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree. I think that's a sound approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can you simply read the handwritten portion that appears on P450, Mr. Kovac's letter. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A combined team of police and judiciary is to deal with the following. Under 1, categorisation; 2, competence of organs; 3, to speed up the procedure. The last word is "sanctions." Whereas there's this one word that I cannot make out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we suggest what the word is? Because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Tieger, if there's a suggestion from those who can read it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We think it's "odgovornosti." How about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, could you have a look at it and, Mr. Mandic, and consider whether that would be a possible ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Odgovornosti, responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not a great surprise, perhaps, in view of 450. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, on -- at least on the face of the enumerated items in the two documents, they appear to have considerable similarity. Can you explain whether or not you detect any differences, significant differences, between the items enumerated in Mr. Kovac's document and the mandate of the two commissions that were formed by the government on August 9th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently, the vice prime minister, Mr. Trbojevic, inserted this document into the agenda and asked that this particular document be acted upon. I believe this to be the handwriting of Mr. Trbojevic, who practically copied verbatim these items here into the conclusions of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to make the record clear, because you were holding the document. When you said in your answer: "Evidently the vice prime minister, Mr. Trbojevic inserted this document," by this document you meant P450, Mr. Kovac's letter of August 8th? If you could just answer affirmatively, Mr. Mandic, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am moving on to a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we had better have a break at this moment. Mr. Mandic, we'll have a break until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you may escort the witness into the courtroom. My attention was drawn during the break to a technical and practical problems in relation to CD-ROMs, but I do understand that it has been explained now, the proper procedure, and that the problem seems to be resolved. That's one. The second matter I'd like to raise is that I again inquired today into what has happened with my specific request to have Mr. Krajisnik provided with a laptop computer in the courtroom, because although I think it's already two weeks ago that I signed the request and that it still has not yet materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First point, Your Honour is right. We think the first point is resolved. Sorry. On the first point, Your Honour, we believe that's resolved. We're awaiting a draft letter with my signature, but since I haven't seen it, I therefore haven't signed it yet. The second point, the laptop computer, it's -- I understood it was physically in the building about ten days ago, so I don't know. But I'll look into it, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I have again drawn the attention to it. Mr. Mandic, please be seated and forgive us for being so impolite to continue to speak when you entered the courtroom. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like next to just draw your attention to a number of documents which bear your name and signature and were issued during the period of time you were minister of justice. The first is a document dated September 3rd, 1992, bearing the ERN 0297-7655.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I note that this document, which is a very brief document of two sentences and bearing four names was disclosed on April 15th -- excuse me. November 15th of this year. If there's any issue in connection with that, we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has no exhibit number yet. It would then be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P452, dated September 3rd, 1992, is directed to the prison administration Vogosca, and states that the inmates listed below need to be transferred to the Kula Penal and Correctional Facility for further procedure. It then lists the names of four persons and indicates that this should be considered a matter of urgency. And was this essentially the directive to the Vogosca prison authorities to transfer detainees or prisoners at Vogosca to Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the Vogosca prison and the Kula prison? Did they fall within the same aspect of the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a temporary facility in Vogosca under the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff of Vogosca. I think that was the case. Or the police. I cannot say exactly. I'm not sure, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I recall you mentioned the other day that Butmir at one point had been under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior and then was taken over by the Ministry of Justice. Was that the same case with Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had closed that facility in Vogosca when we took that over, and up until then, I think it was controlled or run by the police. I'm not sure. I cannot say exactly. I cannot remember who was in charge of Vogosca, which arm of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many detainees or prisoners were being held in Vogosca in September -- at the beginning of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document that we're looking at, P452, refers to further procedure, that is, it indicates that the inmates listed below need to be transferred to Kula for further procedure. What was that further procedure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably for an exchange, but this is not my signature, Mr. Prosecutor, on this document. But it must have been the matter of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise who signed that document on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was done by Slobodan Avlijas, assistant minister for prisons, who was at the same time member of the State Commission set up by the government for investigating the conditions of life and accommodation of prisoners in the whole area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Mandic, can I draw your attention to a document dated September 22nd, 1992, the heading is Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Justice, penal and correctional facility Butmir, and it bears an ERN of ET 0345-6338. That document, Your Honour, was disclosed on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be P453, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, does the late date as such cause you any further -- to make any further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't -- I don't wish to make any specific comment in relation to that particular document and that particular date. It's just -- it's just part of the overall picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P453 is a document directed to district prison Vogosca and it bears your name and a signature. I'll ask you about that signature in a moment. Well, first of all, let me ask you: Is that your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. And there is no register number up there. Probably it was done by an employee of the KP Dom Butmir. I never would have referred to Kula by using the word "Butmir." The correctional facility of Kula. And in addition to that, there was no district prison in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How would you describe or characterise the facility in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, the Crisis Staff and the Territorial Defence and the police set up in Vogosca a prison, and I think the facility was called Sonja [phoen]. That was a catering facility. And in the first half of the first year of the war it existed there, but when we took over Kula in August, then we started closing these other facilities controlled by the army and the police, because everything was transferred to the authority and jurisdiction of the civilian judiciary. And as I said, the penal correctional facility Butmir is not its name at all. There is no register number or archive number, and this is not my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know of other facilities or buildings or locations other than Sonja that were associated with or considered part of the Vogosca facility?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Svrake, there was a facility where non-Serbs were detained, and in the Sonja facility in Vogosca itself. And I think these were two facilities in the area of Vogosca where non-Serbs were incarcerated when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a location or facility or building known as Planjo's house?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it perhaps in the village of Svrake?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I believe so, but I think it would be inappropriate for me -- I need to find out what you know about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about these two facilities in the area of Vogosca municipality, so it means that that would be the other one. There were no other apart from these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you familiar with a man by the name of Branko Vlaco or Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was the chief of police in Vogosca or the commander of the police when the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know what role, if any, he played with respect to these facilities in the Vogosca area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P453 indicates in the third and last sentence of the document: "Therefore, it is necessary to send 50 war prisoners who are in good health to penal and correctional facility Butmir." Do you know why it would have been necessary to specify that only prisoners in good health should be sent to Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with Kula. It has more to do with the economy unit. Because when -- at the beginning of the war, the KP Kula was a semi-open type of prison. This economic unit provided some work, and there were about two hens, egg-laying hens there, 2.000 egg-laying hens, and it was necessary to provide labour for these chicken coops. And I remember that they had about 2.000 egg-laying hens that provided food for the population and the police and the army. There was also a restaurant on the premises of Kula where people could have meals. This is definitely referring to this unit, but this document was prepared by someone from Kula and somebody had obviously misused or abused my signature. It is not customary for the minister, the number-one man in the ministry, to transfer the people to work on this kind of work in an economic unit. There was an assistant minister in charge of these facilities, plus the prison governors were the persons to deal with these kind of matters. This is definitely not my signature, but I know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to a document dated 17 July 1992, bearing the heading "Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Justice Sarajevo." And with the ERN 0301-5749?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 454, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P454 is a decision pursuant to Article 11 of the decision on establishing penal and correctional facilities in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indicating that the minister of justice hereby issues a decision appointing Milorad Krnojelac warden of Foca KP Dom in Foca, a decision that shall enter into force on the day of its adoption. It has your name at the bottom and a signature. First of all, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But in order to avoid any confusion now, I realised who had signed these documents. That was my assistant, Slobodan Avlijas. I was aware of this appointment, because he was in charge of prisons and penal, correctional facilities, and the decision was made to appoint Milorad Krnojelac warden of the Foca KPD. And now I realise who signed on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Mandic. Next can we turn to a document dated August 10th, 1992, bearing the heading Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Justice administration, with the ERN L0102742. This document was disclosed on the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek one clarification, Mr. Tieger. When you said, Mr. Mandic, that you now recognise who signed these documents, would that include the letter sent from Butmir to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P455 appears to be directed to the Serbian municipality of Vogosca War Presidency, Vogosca, with a reference number, your number 03-141/92. And it states: "Regarding your request for the engagement of detainees in works, we hereby inform you that we are in agreement with detainees be temporarily engaged in construction and other works." And it has typewritten your name and minister and then some handwritten notations on the bottom. First of all, Mr. Mandic, do you recall the request and approval to which this document refers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe the translation, instead of temporarily, we believe it should be occasionally, in agreement that detainees be occasionally engaged ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Ms. Cmeric read the relevant words so that we can seek verification with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The relevant word is "povremeno."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Occasionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Cmeric, when I'm almost directly addressing you and requesting you, the Chamber highly appreciates that you're willing to do it. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mandic, can you see the handwritten notation at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and I can read it, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That would be -- that would be great.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot decipher the first word. Then it goes on to say: "Talks were held with the minister on the 10th of August and approval was given." And it was signed again by the man who had sent this letter. On the upper part it says: "Dispatched on the 10th of August, 1992," probably by fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the handwriting or the signature of the man who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was Slobodan Avlijas's signature, because he was the person in charge of prisons and these matters. I am not certain about it, but it does bear his signature. Because you can see that the letter was sent on my behalf. It wasn't signed. But there was this notation saying that on the 10th, this person consulted me and I gave my approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think the first illegible word is "zablijeska [phoen]," which just means "note," apparently. It looks like something fairly harmless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, is that something you could make out of it as well or ...? Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. Thank you, Mr. Stewart, for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Zablijeska, note, that that was correctly put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the document in -- that single sentence refers to detainees occasionally engaged in construction and other works. Do you know what those other works referred to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably other types of construction work. I wouldn't be able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution's next exhibit in order is an intercepted telephone conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Grkovic on July 3rd, 1992. I think there are three clips that are on the Sanction presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will receive a CD-ROM containing these clips. Three clips and one document on one CD? I see that there's nodding from the Prosecution's bench. Then the CD will be 456, the transcript will be 456A and the translation into English will be 456A.1. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If those clips can be played, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we restart playing it so that we get an English and a French transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Radivoje GRKOVIC: It's Grkovic, commander of the Nedzarici battalion. Unknown female person: How may I help you? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Can I speak to one of your superiors? Unknown female person: Which superiors? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Is Momo Mandic there or anyone? Unknown female person: Mandic? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Yes. Unknown female person: Hold on a minute, please. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Radivoje GRKOVIC: God be with you. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Oh, good. Say, a favour, a great favour. Momcilo MANDIC: Go ahead. Radivoje GRKOVIC: I need 30 more Turks. Momcilo MANDIC: Yeah. Radivoje GRKOVIC: For two special tasks. Momcilo MANDIC: Can do. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Can you? Momcilo MANDIC: Sure, I'm sure. Radivoje GRKOVIC: How do I get them here? Momcilo MANDIC: When do you need them? Radivoje GRKOVIC: I'd need them today if you can at all. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. I'll tell Ratko ... Ratko in the afternoon to set aside 30 men so you can come and pick them up. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Well, bro, how will I. Momcilo MANDIC: Is this work obligation? Radivoje GRKOVIC: What work obligation. Special that's what it is. Momcilo MANDIC: Special? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Special. Momcilo MANDIC: Well, let's not do this over the phone. Come over here and Djordje Kalezic is here. He's the errand boy. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Do me a favour. You'll be paid back. I need between 30 and 40 Turks at least. Momcilo MANDIC: Fucking hell, it's 4.30. The people are saying they have to go now. Radivoje GRKOVIC: I know. I know. There will be a payback. Momcilo MANDIC: I don't know how we will ... Radivoje GRKOVIC: There ... Load a big truck or a bus two three guards and drive over here through Pale and Ilijas. Momcilo MANDIC: Is this for an exchange or for work? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Not for an exchange, for special work. I'll tell you -- I can't do it over the phone. Momcilo MANDIC: I know, I know. Fuck. How do we do this? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Please do me that favour Momo. Please, I'm asking you like a brother. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Through Kasindolska and Nedzarici. Momcilo MANDIC: And Nedzarici. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Yes, the barracks. Momcilo MANDIC: The barracks. Radivoje GRKOVIC: If we have 50, that's even better. But 30 or 40 would be ideal. Momcilo MANDIC: Well, I don't -- I don't have transport for them. Hold on a minute. Do you have fuel? Radivoje GRKOVIC: I'll give you oil. Momcilo MANDIC: Oil, huh. Radivoje GRKOVIC: When you come here I'll give you oil. Momcilo MANDIC: Yeah. Yeah. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Is that all right? Momcilo MANDIC: All right. I have that minibus. There are 24 seats. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Perfect, perfect. And two escorts and the driver. Is that all right? Momcilo MANDIC: Hang on. Can the bus pass on the road? Radivoje GRKOVIC: Sure, Momo. Passenger vehicles go there as well. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. I'll think of something. Be there tonight. Radivoje GRKOVIC: I don't have civilian telephone lines. Momcilo MANDIC: What do you mean you don't? Radivoje GRKOVIC: I don't. Everything's blocked where I am, cut off. That's it. Momcilo MANDIC: Well, where are you calling from now? Radivoje GRKOVIC: They phones work at the police station in Ilidza. Momcilo MANDIC: Well, here. We'll then Markovic is here. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Those Turks tonight. Momcilo MANDIC: Tonight. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Tonight. Momcilo MANDIC: Yeah. Radivoje GRKOVIC: My word. Momcilo MANDIC: It's agreed. Radivoje GRKOVIC: Thanks, cheers. Momcilo MANDIC: Cheers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can you tell us first who Mr. Grkovic was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Grkovic was the commander of the Nedzarici barracks, of the barracks in the Sarajevo neighbourhood of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When Mr. Grkovic referred to 30 Turks, who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was he referring to detained Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who were up at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you refer in the conversation to: "All right. I'll tell Ratko, Ratko in the afternoon to set aside 30 men so you can come and pick them up," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratko Lalovic, warden of Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When Mr. Grkovic referred to special tasks for which he wanted the 30 Muslim detainees, what was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was referring to, but I think that it might have been the fortifying of the Nedzarici barracks. I do not know this for a fact. I believe so. Probably digging trenches and fortifying the barracks held by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like next to turn to Prosecution's next in order, a bulletin dated 19 September 1992 and bearing the ERN L0103035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P457, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document was disclosed on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P457 bears the heading Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian municipality of Vogosca prison department and it states: "Pursuant to order number 11/84, dated 17 September 1992, and at the request of brigade commander Mladen Trifunovic, 50 prisoners were taken to Zuc hill to carry out works." And then it goes on to indicate that in the course of the works the following were killed by the enemy, naming four persons, and the following prisoners were wounded on the same day, listing seven persons. There's an indication that there was an attachment, including a list order and a statement, and it bears the -- the signatory is the prison warden, Branko Vlaco, and it has a signature.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, is that the same Branko Vlaco to whom you referred a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. There was a large family of Vlaco at Vogosca, so he might be a member of the family. I'm not certain. I know that there was a chief of police before the war. This was a man by the name of Vlaco. Whether his first name was Branko or not, I don't know. This family lived in the area of Vogosca, and so there are quite a few Vlacos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the document indicates that at the request of the brigade commander, Mladen Trifunovic, there was an order, and the date of that order. 50 prisoners were taken to Zuc hill to carry out works. Can you tell us what you know about the nature of the works that were -- that those prisoners were tasked to carry out?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Vlaco was -- appeared here on behalf of the Vogosca municipality prison department and he received a request to send 50 prisoners for the purposes of the army. Because under the army law, in a period of an immediate threat of war, the army was entitled to be given at its disposal all the prisoners held in prisons, regardless of whether the prisoners were controlled by the army, the police, or civilian organs. They would issue orders, verbally or in writing, for such men to be given at their disposal and would return these people back to the prisons after the end of the task. That was the Zuc hill where fighting was going on between the Serb and the Muslim armies, and most probably these people were taken there to dig trenches on the separation line. So they had the authority to pick out people from whichever prison they wanted in order to use them for the purposes of defence or whatever other military purposes they had, and this was something that was here referred to by Vlaco Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The order that is referred to in the first sentence of the bulletin, that is, number 11/84, do you understand that to be an order that came from Vlaco in response to the request to the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who could have issued the order. Perhaps the War Presidency of the Vogosca municipality. I'm not certain as to the authority issuing this order. Perhaps the military command at Vogosca. I wouldn't know. Evidently, Mladen Trifunovic issued a request for Zuc hill. Now, who issued the order, whether it was the army, the civilian authorities, or Vlaco himself, I don't know. I am not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are you able to determine the ethnicity of the prisoners who were killed and wounded by the names that are listed on the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Muslims. And it is evident that these were prisoners of war. Mr. Prosecutor, it says here that while they were performing their work, they were killed. So it must have been on the -- along the separation line during the combat activities between the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, can we turn next to a telephone conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Ratko Mladic on 24 May 1992, which was previously marked an entered as P154A, tab 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you for the transcript inform -- my assistance, repeat the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll look it up again to make sure I'm repeating it correctly, Your Honour. Tab 33. And for the benefit of the booth, and I apologise for not mentioning that when I identified the exhibit, this is an item in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mandic, do you recognise the participants in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The participants are General Ratko Mladic and Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know the -- let me say first. Mr. Krajisnik asks General Mladic in an earlier portion of the conversation whether or not you had arrived down there. General Mladic indicates that you were there today but it appears that you have left. And Mr. Krajisnik indicates that you will come down there. And General Mladic indicates: Yes. First of all, do you recall the -- well, let me ask you: Do you know what issues were being addressed by General Mladic and Mr. Krajisnik in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this took place at the time when General Ratko Mladic was at Lukavica, at the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks, and that quite possibly the instant matter was the moving out or the dislocation of the army from the Marsal Tito and Viktor Bubanj barracks in Sarajevo. That's what I think this is about, about dislocating those children, the recruits, from these two barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall receiving information from Mr. Krajisnik and conveying it to General Mladic about the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a bit confusing, because Momcilo Krajisnik said that he was supposed to convey some information to me, meaning really to me, and he was addressing Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we -- I see it's getting late, Your Honour. I'll make this the last question I ask. If we look a little bit farther down in the conversation, after Mr. Krajisnik asked if you have arrived down there and General Mladic indicates that you had been there previously. But it appeared you had left, Mr. Krajisnik states: "I have to give him some information," appearing to refer to you as "him." And then he says: "And now I'll try and see if there's a guy with a jeep here."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then he says, "please when he arrives," a piece of information that he conveys is related to this information. Does that shed any light on who was giving you information in connection with this conversation and what you were to do with the information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this has to do with the dislocation of these two barracks from the federal Sarajevo, because at that time, that was my only reason to be in contact with Mladic. Because the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks where Ratko Mladic was for a period of time is very close to -- or was very close to the line of contact, line of separation. Some 500 metres away, that's where the district court and the Kula prison were, and all the other institutions of justice administration. So I probably went up to Pale, to Jahorina hotel, but I don't remember what sort of information Krajisnik was supposed to convey to me, perhaps related to my family - I did have some problems there at this period of time - or whether the information had to do with the dislocation of these barracks that were encircled, the Viktor Bubanj and the Marsal Tito barracks that found themselves in a difficult situation at the time. But I cannot recall at present.
